newsitem.title: EGYPT: Mubarak says renegotiating deals dangerous.
newsitem.headline: Mubarak says renegotiating deals dangerous.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak said on Sunday Israel's insistence on renegotiating issues it had agreed upon with Palestinians was dangerous and could throw the region into catastrophe.

But the Egyptian leader, whose country became the first Arab nation to sign a peace deal with Israel in 1979, said in a television interview just hours before Palestinians and Israelis were to resume peace talks in the Gaza Strip that he hoped the two sides could find a way to implement their peace agreements.

The Gaza talks, with the participation of the United States Middle East envoy Dennis Ross, centre on an Israeli redeployment from the West Bank city of Hebron delayed since March by Islamic suicide bombings that killed 59 people and by Israeli security concerns.
Israel's hardline Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu views Israeli-PLO peace accords as fundamentally flawed but promises to see the Hebron redeployment through as an international committment.

"There are agreements that were signed with the late prime minister Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres. Netanyahu came along and does not want to implement them. He says he wants to implement them and that he is committed but until now there is nothing," Mubarak said.

"He says let's start negotiations. But negotiations on what? I know that the talks that should start are those on the final status of the issue but redeployment from Hebron has already been talked about and finished in difficult negotiations and they reached agreement and even the means to implement them.

"The priniciple of renegotiation is a dangerous one. These are agreements that are internationally recognised that were signed here in Egypt and in the United States. One must respect them or there will be a catastrophe," Mubarak added.
Sunday's talks in the Palestinian-ruled Gaza Strip are the outcome of last week's emergency White House summit spurred by bloody clashes in which 58 Palestinians and 15 Israelis died.
The violence began after Israel opened a new entrance to a controversial tunnel near Jerusalem's al-Aqsa mosque, Islam's third holiest site.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher arrived in the Middle East on Sunday to urge Palestinians and Israelis to reach swift results in their talks.

Mubarak boycotted the Washington summit because of what he called Israel's intransigence and its poor treatment of Palestinians. Egypt has often mediated in peace talks between Israel and its Arab neighbours but it has recently been locked in a war of words with the Jewish state.
Mubarak said the Washington talks -- deemed a failure by Palestinians, Arabs and most Europeans -- could have achieved more if Netanyahu had been more flexible.
"If he (Netanyahu) had more political flexibility they would have been able to achieve more than they did in Washington."
